output.intent: 6 weeks of focused hypertrophy: Full Body ×2 trains every muscle about twice a week inside the 10–20 weekly hard-set band, adding reps and load as you earn them. The plan is to build for 4 weeks, then deload and reassess.
output.progression: Week 1 is an introduction: run the prescribed sets and reps at a weight you could clearly do 4–5 more reps with. Nothing is being tested — you are teaching your body the movements so the following weeks can be hard. Start each new lift lighter than feels necessary — a weight you could do 3–4 more reps with — and focus on clean, controlled form. Each session, if you hit the top of the rep range with good technique, add the smallest jump (usually 5 lbs, or 2.5 lbs on smaller lifts) next time. As a beginner this simple "add a little every week" progression works for months — the coach handles the bookkeeping and eases you back if a weight gets away from you. Week 6 is a planned deload — roughly 10% lighter across the board — so the rebound lands inside this block, not after it. Muscle Growth stays the destination — just keep showing up.

output.progression: Week 1 is an introduction: run the prescribed sets and reps at a weight you could clearly do 4–5 more reps with. Nothing is being tested — you are teaching your body the movements so the following weeks can be hard. Start each new lift lighter than feels necessary — a weight you could do 3–4 more reps with — and focus on clean, controlled form. Each session, if you hit the top of the rep range with good technique, add the smallest jump (usually 5 lbs, or 2.5 lbs on smaller lifts) next time. As a beginner this simple "add a little every week" progression works for months — the coach handles the bookkeeping and eases you back if a weight gets away from you. Week 6 is a planned deload — roughly 10% lighter across the board — so the rebound lands inside this block, not after it. Fat Loss stays the destination — just keep showing up.

phaseNotes: You're starting out, so the block opens with an introductory week: same movements, easy loads, no chasing numbers. Technique first is not a formality — it is what makes the following weeks trainable.
Week 1 is an introduction — same movements, easy loads. Adding lifting to an endurance week is a new stress in itself; the first week is for learning the lifts, not testing them.
Weeks 2–3 carry the strength work — heavy, low-volume, well short of failure. This is the part of the block where lifting is allowed to cost you something.
Weeks 4–5 hold the loads and cut the sets. Your triathlon training is the priority from here; lifting exists to stop you losing what you built.

Two or three sessions a week of heavy, low-volume, multi-joint lifting is the dose the concurrent-training research supports for endurance athletes — enough to raise maximal strength, cheap enough that your sport keeps its recovery.
Every main lift stops two to three reps short of failure. The strength adaptation does not need the last rep; your next session does need the recovery it would cost.
Volume sits well under a bodybuilding dose on purpose: added muscle mass is weight you carry for the whole race, and rising tonnage is a cost here rather than a sign of progress.
Olympic: Olympic distance still rewards heavy strength work, and your weekly sport hours leave room for it. Main lifts run at 4–6 reps.
Swim is your weak link, so the upper day adds a straight-arm pulling slot on top of the vertical pull.
Knee history noted — box jumps are out, squatting moves to supported variations, and hip abduction stays in as the direct fix for the pelvic control that usually drives runner's knee.
output.intent: 6 weeks of lifting in service of your triathlon: Strength · Unilateral keeps the sessions short, heavy and well short of failure. The plan is to build strength early, then hold it through your heaviest training weeks so your sport gets the recovery back. If a session ever clashes with a quality triathlon workout, the triathlon workout wins — that is not a compromise, it is the design.
output.progression: Week 1 is an introduction: run the prescribed sets and reps at a weight you could clearly do 4–5 more reps with. Nothing is being tested — you are teaching your body the movements so the following weeks can be hard. Load climbs on the main lifts whenever you own the top of the rep range with two or three reps still in the tank. If a set feels like a grind, it was too heavy — stop the set, not the session. From week 4 the loads stop climbing and the sets come down. That is deliberate: strength is defended by intensity, and the volume is what your triathlon training needs back. Week 6 backs off — same kind of weight, a third of the work. The coach will never add sets to this plan. It can trim them, and it will if your logged sessions say you are running out of road.

output.splitReason: Two days — the dose the research keeps validating for endurance athletes. One heavy bilateral session, one single-leg and pulling session, both under 45 minutes.
phaseNotes: You're starting out, so the block opens with an introductory week: same movements, easy loads, no chasing numbers. Technique first is not a formality — it is what makes the following weeks trainable.
Week 1 is an introduction — same movements, easy loads. Adding lifting to an endurance week is a new stress in itself; the first week is for learning the lifts, not testing them.
Weeks 2–3 carry the strength work — heavy, low-volume, well short of failure. This is the part of the block where lifting is allowed to cost you something.
Weeks 4–4 hold the loads and cut the sets. Your triathlon training is the priority from here; lifting exists to stop you losing what you built.

decisions.name: Leg Press
decisions.reason: Supported knee-extension work with a controlled range — the strength still transfers, and the joint gets a say in the depth.

decisions.name: Cable Pull Through
decisions.reason: Posterior-chain strength is the best-supported protective factor for the run leg, and it powers the top of the pedal stroke.

decisions.name: Seated Calf Raises
decisions.reason: Bent-knee calf work loads the soleus — the largest force contributor in running gait, and the tissue most often under-prepared for it. Three seconds down on every rep.

decisions.name: Dead Bug
decisions.reason: Anti-rotation strength holds the aero position without leaking power, and keeps your pelvis honest as the run wears on.

decisions.name: Dumbbell Step Up
decisions.reason: Loaded single-leg hip extension is the closest the gym gets to a pedal stroke, and it exposes the side-to-side asymmetry bilateral lifting hides.

decisions.name: Single Leg Romanian Deadlift
decisions.reason: Hamstring strength plus pelvic control in one movement — the combination that holds up in the back half of a run.

decisions.name: Lat Pull Down
decisions.reason: Vertical pulling strength for the catch — the phase of the stroke where propulsion is actually generated.

decisions.name: Seated Cable Row
decisions.reason: Postural counterweight to the hours you spend folded over the bars.

decisions.name: Dumbbell External Rotation
decisions.reason: Light external rotation balances the internally-rotated pull of swim volume. Two or three kilos is plenty — this slot is insurance, not training.

decisions.name: Straight Arm Pull Downs
decisions.reason: Straight-arm pulling mirrors the front of the catch, where a weak swim usually loses its water.

guidanceNotes: Notes saved with the plan — review the workouts below and swap anything that doesn't fit.

Two or three sessions a week of heavy, low-volume, multi-joint lifting is the dose the concurrent-training research supports for endurance athletes — enough to raise maximal strength, cheap enough that your sport keeps its recovery.
Every main lift stops two to three reps short of failure. The strength adaptation does not need the last rep; your next session does need the recovery it would cost.
Volume sits well under a bodybuilding dose on purpose: added muscle mass is weight you carry for the whole race, and rising tonnage is a cost here rather than a sign of progress.
Olympic: Olympic distance still rewards heavy strength work, and your weekly sport hours leave room for it. Main lifts run at 4–6 reps.

Two or three sessions a week of heavy, low-volume, multi-joint lifting is the dose the concurrent-training research supports for endurance athletes — enough to raise maximal strength, cheap enough that your sport keeps its recovery.
Every main lift stops two to three reps short of failure. The strength adaptation does not need the last rep; your next session does need the recovery it would cost.
Volume sits well under a bodybuilding dose on purpose: added muscle mass is weight you carry for the whole race, and rising tonnage is a cost here rather than a sign of progress.
Olympic: Olympic distance still rewards heavy strength work, and your weekly sport hours leave room for it. Main lifts run at 4–6 reps.
Swim is your weak link, so the upper day adds a straight-arm pulling slot on top of the vertical pull.
Knee history noted — box jumps are out, squatting moves to supported variations, and hip abduction stays in as the direct fix for the pelvic control that usually drives runner's knee.
output.intent: 8 weeks of lifting in service of your triathlon: Strength · Unilateral keeps the sessions short, heavy and well short of failure. The plan is to build strength early, then hold it through your heaviest training weeks so your sport gets the recovery back. If a session ever clashes with a quality triathlon workout, the triathlon workout wins — that is not a compromise, it is the design.
output.progression: Week 1 is an introduction: run the prescribed sets and reps at a weight you could clearly do 4–5 more reps with. Nothing is being tested — you are teaching your body the movements so the following weeks can be hard. Load climbs on the main lifts whenever you own the top of the rep range with two or three reps still in the tank. If a set feels like a grind, it was too heavy — stop the set, not the session. From week 6 the loads stop climbing and the sets come down. That is deliberate: strength is defended by intensity, and the volume is what your triathlon training needs back. Week 8 backs off — same kind of weight, a third of the work. The coach will never add sets to this plan. It can trim them, and it will if your logged sessions say you are running out of road.

Every main lift stops two to three reps short of failure. The strength adaptation does not need the last rep; your next session does need the recovery it would cost.
Volume sits well under a bodybuilding dose on purpose: added muscle mass is weight you carry for the whole race, and rising tonnage is a cost here rather than a sign of progress.

Marathon: Marathon mileage is the training; lifting exists to keep you intact through it. No jumping, a minimum effective dose at 6–8 reps, and the volume that remains goes to calves, hamstrings and hip stabilisers — where marathon injuries actually happen.
output.intent: 8 weeks of lifting in service of your running: Strength · Durability keeps the sessions short, heavy and well short of failure. The plan is to build strength early, then hold it through your heaviest training weeks so your sport gets the recovery back. If a session ever clashes with a quality running workout, the running workout wins — that is not a compromise, it is the design.
output.progression: Week 1 is an introduction: run the prescribed sets and reps at a weight you could clearly do 4–5 more reps with. Nothing is being tested — you are teaching your body the movements so the following weeks can be hard. Load climbs on the main lifts whenever you own the top of the rep range with two or three reps still in the tank. If a set feels like a grind, it was too heavy — stop the set, not the session. From week 3 the loads stop climbing and the sets come down. That is deliberate: strength is defended by intensity, and the volume is what your running training needs back. Week 7 backs off — same kind of weight, a third of the work. The coach will never add sets to this plan. It can trim them, and it will if your logged sessions say you are running out of road.
warnings: You asked for 4 lifting days, but at 8–11 hours of running a week the plan uses 2. Lifting that costs you a quality session in your sport is a net loss — the extra day is better spent recovering.
At 8–11 hours of running a week there is only room for a minimum effective dose, so one accessory slot was dropped (Upper Back). The heavy lifts are what defend your strength — those stay.

output.splitReason: Two days — the dose the research keeps validating for endurance athletes. One heavy bilateral session, one single-leg and hip-durability session, both under 45 minutes.
phaseNotes: Weeks 1–3 carry the strength work — heavy, low-volume, well short of failure. This is the part of the block where lifting is allowed to cost you something.
Weeks 4–10 hold the loads and cut the sets. Your running training is the priority from here; lifting exists to stop you losing what you built.

Weeks 11–12 are a taper: one short session a week, roughly 10% lighter, at the bottom of every rep range. You will not lose strength in a fortnight, and arriving at the start line with fresh legs is worth far more than the training those weeks would have bought.
In race week itself, lift once early if at all, and nothing inside 72 hours of the start.

decisions.name: Barbell Back Squat
decisions.reason: Heavy bilateral squatting is the most reliable route to better running economy — more force per stride means each one costs a smaller share of your ceiling.

decisions.name: Romanian Deadlifts
decisions.reason: Hamstring strength is the single best-supported protective factor in running, and it drives hip extension through toe-off.

decisions.name: Seated Calf Raises
decisions.reason: Bent-knee calf raises load the soleus, which absorbs more force per stride than any other muscle in the chain and is the tissue most often under-prepared for it. Three seconds down on every rep.

decisions.name: Pallof Press
decisions.reason: Anti-rotation strength keeps your pelvis from giving way as the miles accumulate — the point where form and economy fall apart together.

decisions.name: Bulgarian Split Squat
decisions.reason: Running is a single-leg sport, and loaded single-leg work exposes the side-to-side asymmetry bilateral lifting hides.

decisions.name: Single Leg Romanian Deadlift
decisions.reason: Hamstring strength plus pelvic control in one movement — the combination that holds up in the last few miles.

decisions.name: Hip Abduction
decisions.reason: Glute-med strength controls the pelvis through every stance phase — the cheapest insurance there is against ITB pain and a sore kneecap.

decisions.name: Single Leg Calf Raise
decisions.reason: Straight-leg, single-leg calf work covers the gastrocnemius and the Achilles at the load a stride actually applies — one leg at a time, because that is how you run.

decisions.name: Dead Bug

decisions.name: Dumbbell Step Up

decisions.name: Single Leg Romanian Deadlift

decisions.name: Lat Pull Down

decisions.name: Dumbbell External Rotation

decisions.reason: Lateral trunk stability under single-leg load. Logged in seconds — build the hold, not the reps.

guidanceNotes: Notes saved with the plan — review the workouts below and swap anything that doesn't fit.

Two or three sessions a week of heavy, low-volume, multi-joint lifting is the dose the concurrent-training research supports for endurance athletes — enough to raise maximal strength, cheap enough that your sport keeps its recovery.
Every main lift stops two to three reps short of failure. The strength adaptation does not need the last rep; your next session does need the recovery it would cost.
Volume sits well under a bodybuilding dose on purpose: added muscle mass is weight you carry for the whole race, and rising tonnage is a cost here rather than a sign of progress.
Sprint: Sprint distance is short and hard, so maximal strength and rate of force development transfer directly. Main lifts stay heavy at 4–6 reps and the power session earns its place.
Bike is your weak link, so the single-leg step-up carries an extra set — unilateral hip extension is the most direct strength transfer to sustained pedalling power.
Achilles/calf history noted — the jumping is out and calf work is loaded heavy and slow instead. Reintroduce hops only once it is quiet for a few weeks.
Shoulder history noted — nothing goes overhead, and the rotation work gets an extra set because that is the part that actually helps.
output.intent: 12 weeks of lifting in service of your triathlon: Strength · Unilateral keeps the sessions short, heavy and well short of failure. The plan is to build strength while it is cheap to build — there is no race close enough for that to cost you anything. If a session ever clashes with a quality triathlon workout, the triathlon workout wins — that is not a compromise, it is the design.
output.progression: Load climbs on the main lifts whenever you own the top of the rep range with two or three reps still in the tank. If a set feels like a grind, it was too heavy — stop the set, not the session. The coach will never add sets to this plan. It can trim them, and it will if your logged sessions say you are running out of road.
warnings: You asked for 4 lifting days, but at under 4 hours of triathlon a week the plan uses 3. Lifting that costs you a quality session in your sport is a net loss — the extra day is better spent recovering.
